newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - PC Baby gets a rebuild for 50th birthday.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - PC Baby gets a rebuild for 50th birthday.

text.p: Nicknamed "The Baby", the world's first programmable computer was a cumbersome giant that took up the space of a large room.

When her three inventors brought her to life at Manchester University in the north of England in 1948, they took a step forward that was to revolutionise the 20th century by paving the way for the modern personal computer.
Baby, a tangle of wiring and crude electronic valves, was gradually dismantled and forgotten about as the silicon chip was developed, enabling smaller, faster machines to be built.

Determined to secure her a place in history, a team of computer enthusiasts have ventured back to the roots of their science -- and the very laboratory where she was built -- in order to reconstruct Baby in time for her 50th birthday next June.
They are just weeks away from their goal.
"We're ploughing along, and we're well on schedule for the birthday party next year," project leader Chris Burton told Reuters in an interview.
Large-scale celebrations are planned for June 21 1998 -- the day the first program ran on the world's first fully programmable electronic digital computer.
"A TRIUMPH OF BRITISH INNOVATION"

"Baby was a triumph of British innovation," said Burton, a retired computer engineer. "Today's computers are smaller, faster and much more powerful than Baby, but they work on exactly the same principle."
Burton has had to rely on a 50-year-old notebook of scribbled circuit diagrams and a pile of yellowed photographs to piece together the replica.

He spent months hunting down old electronic valves in collectors' attics across Britain, and even tracked down the original metal racks which had ended up propping up a flowerbed in somebody's back garden.
Baby's memory was only 1,024 bits, much weaker than most modern computers which boast around 164 million bits.

"With a memory of that size, you couldn't run any of today's programs, except maybe a very basic version of a game like chess," said Colin Wilson, applications development manager at software company Erdas UK.
Nevertheless, Baby had seven types of instruction loop, meaning that with a bigger memory she would have been capable of running the most sophisticated programs.

Earlier computers like Colossus, the street-sized code-cracking machine built by British inventor Charles Babbage around 1943, and in 1946 ENIAC -- the U.S. Army's number-crunching computer -- did not have Baby's stored program facility. Both had to be reprogrammed manually before a new program could be executed.
"BABY" BUILT TO TEST STORED MEMORY
Baby was not originally intended to rival these, but was built by Dr. Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill to test out a stored memory being designed by the late British professor, Freddie Williams.
"The interest was to build a digital memory that you could read and write electronically," said Dai Edwards, who helped out with the project as a 20-year-old student.
"Having designed the memory we needed to test it. The idea was to build a machine in which you could input not just numbers but codes which could be interpreted as instructions."
The memory used cathode ray tubes to store data as charged points on a screen. An electron beam scanned the points, allocated binary ones or zeros, and could then read the information back on demand.
Tucked between Baby's huge racks of circuit wiring were a vertical keyboard for inputing instructions and a screen displaying the results as glowing green dots.
As the inventors realised the importance of their creation, the pace intensified to run the first program.
"It was a moment to remember," is how Kilburn described producing the first set of results.
Early trials had produced a "random dance" of light points on the screen. But on June 21, 1948, something different happened.
"There, shining brightly in the expected place, was the expected answer," Kilburn said. "Nothing was ever the same again."
News of Baby's debut quickly hit the headlines. She was hailed as: "A marvel of our time -- the memory machine which can solve the most complex mathematical problems".
Her inventors were bombarded with letters from DNA crystallographers, weather forecasters and atomic energy researchers who had mathematical calculations which were too lengthy to solve by hand.
"They had problems to solve and we were interested in making computers. It was a meeting of two sets of enthusiasts," said Edwards.

Baby was developed by Ferranti Ltd. to become the Mark 1 computer and was sold commercially. By 1951 the original baby machine had been taken apart as the university team moved on to further achievements.
SILICON CHIP A TURNING POINT FOR COMPUTERS
The introduction of the silicon chip was a turning point for modern computers.

Thousands of transistors necessary for storing information could be crammed onto a tiny silicon chip, whereas a few thousand of the old-fashioned transistor valves required racks reaching up to the ceiling.
So why rebuild this old relic?

Burton, whose former employer International Computers Ltd backed the project, said that, while he wanted to recognise the pioneers who brought about the "second industrial revolution", a second motive was educational.
"We wanted to provide a snapshot of what it was like 50 years ago so that scholars can look back and see what things were like then," said Burton.
Erdas's Wilson said rebuilding Baby was useful as an educational exercise.
"It's a bit like putting Stonehenge back together," he said, referring to a prehistoric circle of sacred stones in the south of England.
Wilson said advances in the next 50 years would be a world apart from Baby, with interactive computers and holographic 3-D screens becoming a real possibility.

Once Baby's replica is complete, the engineers will dismantle it, transport it to Manchester's Museum of Science and Industry and set it up all over again as the centrepiece in the communications gallery there.
